overview.text: Ammonia (NH₃) is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, normally a colorless gas with a sharp, pungent odor. In water it acts as a weak base, accepting a hydrogen ion from water to form ammonium and hydroxide ions. This behavior helps make aqueous ammonia useful in cleaning products. Its largest industrial role is supplying nitrogen for fertilizers, supporting plant growth. Manufacturers synthesize it by reacting nitrogen and hydrogen at elevated temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst in the Haber–Bosch process. Ammonia is also used to make nitric acid, refrigerants, and other chemicals; if released or mismanaged, it can harm aquatic ecosystems.

key_facts.text: Ammonia’s formula is NH₃: each molecule contains one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.
In water, ammonia is a weak base: only some molecules react to form ammonium and hydroxide ions.
The Haber–Bosch reaction combines nitrogen and hydrogen with an iron catalyst under elevated temperature and pressure: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
Ammonia is used in fertilizers and in making products including nitric acid, household cleaners, and refrigerants.
Ammonia entering surface waters can act as a nutrient, but high concentrations can harm aquatic life.
